claim: Fatal Familial Insomnia (FFI) is a genetic prion disease caused by the D178N mutation in the prion protein gene (PRNP) in coupling phase with methionine at PRNP 129.
source: Fatal Familial Insomnia (FFI) is a genetic prion disease caused by the D178N mutation in the prion protein gene (PRNP) in coupling phase with methionine at PRNP 129.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: In 2017, the olfactory mucosa (OM) collected from FFI patients contained traces of PrPSc detectable by Protein Misfolding Cyclic Amplification (PMCA).
source: In 2017, we have shown that the olfactory mucosa (OM) collected from FFI patients contained traces of PrPSc detectable by Protein Misfolding Cyclic Amplification (PMCA).
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors (Redaelli et al., 2017) cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: All inoculated BvPrP-Tg407 mice with FFI-related materials developed mild spongiform changes, astroglial activation, and PrPSc deposition mainly affecting the thalamus.
source: All inoculated mice developed mild spongiform changes, astroglial activation, and PrPSc deposition mainly affecting the thalamus.
evidence: This is supported by histological and immunohistochemical data presented in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: The neuropathological alterations in mice inoculated with PMCA products were different from those found in mice injected with raw FFI brain homogenate.
source: However, their neuropathological alterations were different from those found in the brain of BvPrP-Tg407 mice injected with raw FFI brain homogenate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing histological patterns shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7 across different inoculation groups.

claim: PrPSc present in OM of FFI patients is potentially infectious.
source: Although with some experimental constraints, we show that PrPSc present in OM of FFI patients is potentially infectious.
evidence: This is supported by the successful transmission of disease to mice inoculated with FFI-OM_PMCA products.

claim: The cause of FFI is an autosomal-dominant mutation at codon 178 of the PRNP gene, resulting in aspartic acid (D) to asparagine (N) substitution (D178N).
source: In 1992, it was shown that the cause of the disease is an autosomal-dominant mutation at codon 178 of the PrPC encoding gene (PRNP), resulting in aspartic acid (D) to asparagine (N) substitution (D178N) (Medori et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citation to Medori et al., 1992.

claim: FFI pathology primarily affects the thalamus, showing neuronal loss, spongiform changes, astrogliosis, and moderate PrPSc deposition.
source: The pathology primarily affects the thalamus that shows neuronal loss, spongiform changes, astrogliosis, and moderate PrPSc deposition (Montagna et al., 2003; Macchi et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on FFI pathology.

claim: The polymorphism at codon 129 of the PRNP (methionine [M] or valine [V]) plays a significant role in disease heterogeneity.
source: The polymorphism at codon 129 of the PRNP (methionine [M] or valine [V]) plays a significant role in disease heterogeneity (Monari et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Monari et al., 1994 and further elaborated with specific examples.

claim: FFID178N-129MM causes FFI with rapid progression (7–18 months), sleep disturbances, and dysautonomia.
source: For instance, the presence of MM (FFID178N-129MM) causes FFI with rapid progression (7–18 months), sleep disturbances, and dysautonomia.
evidence: This is a description of clinical phenotype associated with specific genotype, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: FFID178N-129MV is associated with longer disease duration (20–35 months) with equilibrium and gait dysfunctions.
source: The presence of MV (FFID178N-129MV) is associated with longer disease duration (20–35 months) with equilibrium and gait dysfunctions
evidence: This describes the clinical phenotype for the MV genotype, based on established knowledge.

claim: The presence of VV at codon 129 causes a distinct genetic disease, referred to as familial Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (fCJDD178N-129VV).
source: while the presence of VV causes a distinct genetic disease, referred to as familial Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (fCJDD178N-129VV) (Gambetti et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gambetti et al., 1995.

claim: Codon 129 polymorphism in PRNP does not influence the age at disease onset.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that codon 129 polymorphism in PRNP does not influence the age at disease onset (Montagna et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Montagna et al., 2006.

claim: PrPC is synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum where it undergoes several post-translation modifications.
source: PrPC is synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum where it undergoes several post-translation modifications, including the addition of a GPI anchor to its C-terminal part, the formation of a disulfide bridge between two cysteine residues (Cys179-Cys214), and the N-linked glycosylation at two asparagine residues (Asn181 and Asn197) (Turk et al., 1988).
evidence: This describes the biosynthesis of PrPC, supported by citation to Turk et al., 1988.

claim: In the Golgi apparatus, the oligosaccharides of PrPC are modified to produce complex-type chains rich in sialic acid.
source: Finally, in the Golgi apparatus, the oligosaccharides are modified to produce complex-type chains rich in sialic acid (Caughey et al., 1989), which have an important role in targeting PrPC to neuronal synapses (Bate et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Caughey et al., 1989 and Bate et al., 2016.

claim: The pattern of glycosylation gives rise to different PrPC forms: the di-glycosylated (70%), the mono-glycosylated (25%), and the un-glycosylated (5%) species.
source: The pattern of glycosylation gives rise to different PrPC forms: the di-glycosylated (70%), the mono-glycosylated (25%), and the un-glycosylated (5%) species (Caughey et al., 1989; Rudd et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Caughey et al., 1989 and Rudd et al., 1999.

claim: All PrPC species are soluble in detergent and sensitive to proteinase K (PK) digestion.
source: All PrPC species are soluble in detergent and sensitive to proteinase K (PK) digestion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the biochemical properties of PrPC.

claim: The D178N mutation reduces the structural stability of the PrPC, which is more prone to convert into PrPSc and aggregate.
source: The D178N mutation reduces the structural stability of the PrPC, which is more prone to convert into PrPSc and aggregate (Liemann and Glockshuber, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liemann and Glockshuber, 1999.

claim: PrPSc is less soluble in detergent and is partially resistant to PK digestion.
source: This latter is less soluble in detergent and is partially resistant to PK digestion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the biochemical properties of PrPSc.

claim: After PK treatment, the resistant un-glycosylated band of PrPSc associated with FFID178N-129MM or FFID178N-129MV shows a molecular weight of 19 kDa.
source: After PK treatment, the resistant un-glycosylated band of PrPSc associated with FFID178N-129MM or FFID178N-129MV shows a molecular weight of 19 kDa, while that associated with fCJDD178N-129VV has a molecular weight of 21 kDa (Monari et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Monari et al., 1994.

claim: The un-glycosylated band of PrPSc associated with fCJDD178N-129VV has a molecular weight of 21 kDa.
source: After PK treatment, the resistant un-glycosylated band of PrPSc associated with FFID178N-129MM or FFID178N-129MV shows a molecular weight of 19 kDa, while that associated with fCJDD178N-129VV has a molecular weight of 21 kDa (Monari et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Monari et al., 1994.

claim: The mutation at position 178 and the polymorphism at 129 of the PRNP affect the tertiary structure of the protein, thus influencing the cleavage of PK at the N-terminal region.
source: These differences suggest that the mutation at position 178 and the polymorphism at 129 of the PRNP affect the tertiary structure of the protein, thus influencing the cleavage of PK at the N-terminal region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in molecular weight after PK treatment.

claim: Alterations in PrPSc structure might be the factor responsible for the phenotypic heterogeneity of FFI.
source: Such alterations in PrPSc structure might be the factor responsible for the phenotypic heterogeneity of FFI.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the relationship between PrPSc structure and disease phenotype.

claim: Mice genetically modified to express murine PrP with the D177N mutation generate spontaneous prion pathology where PrPSc is barely detectable.
source: The ability of the D178N mutation to promote conversion of PrPC into PrPSc that results in the generation of spontaneous prion pathology was shown in mice genetically modified to express murine PrP with the D177N mutation (the equivalent to human D178N) where PrPSc is barely detectable (Bouybayoune et al., 2015; Jackson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bouybayoune et al., 2015 and Jackson et al., 2009.

claim: The infectious properties of FFI-PrPSc were extensively investigated by transmission studies in wild-type animals and several lines of mice genetically modified to express human PrP as well as primates.
source: The infectious properties of FFI-PrPSc were extensively investigated by transmission studies in wild-type animals (Tateishi et al., 1995; Sasaki et al., 2005) and in several lines of mice genetically modified to express human PrP (Telling et al., 1994; Telling et al., 1995) as well as primates (Tateishi et al., 1995; Brown et al., 1994; Collinge et al., 1995; Telling et al., 1996; Takeuchi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to transmission studies.

claim: Several factors, including the polymorphisms at codon 129 of the incoming FFI-PrPSc inoculum, the prion titer of the FFI brain areas used to challenge the animals, and the PrPC amino acid sequence of the recipient animals, could significantly influence the transmission efficiency.
source: Results of these studies showed that several factors, including the polymorphisms at codon 129 of the incoming FFI-PrPSc inoculum, the prion titer of the FFI brain areas used to challenge the animals, and the PrPC amino acid sequence of the recipient animals, could significantly influence the transmission efficiency.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple transmission studies cited in the previous sentence.

claim: When inoculated in mice expressing a chimeric human-mouse PrP, FFI-PrPSc is able to promote the generation of prions characterized by similar biochemical features of the original inoculum.
source: Notably, when inoculated in mice expressing a chimeric human-mouse PrP, FFI-PrPSc is able to promote the generation of prions characterized by similar biochemical features of the original inoculum (Telling et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Telling et al., 1996.

claim: FFI was efficiently transmitted to knock-in mice expressing the bank vole PrP with methionine at codon 109 of the PrPC.
source: In a recent report, FFI was efficiently transmitted to knock-in mice expressing the bank vole PrP (BvPrP) with methionine at codon 109 of the PrPC (Takeuchi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takeuchi et al., 2019.

claim: The PrPSc generated in bank vole knock-in mice showed the typical biochemical features of FFI-PrPSc (predominance of the di-glycosylated band and migration of the un-glycosylated PrP species at 19 kDa).
source: Also in this case, the PrPSc generated in mice showed the typical biochemical features of FFI-PrPSc (predominance of the di-glycosylated band and migration of the un-glycosylated PrP species at 19 kDa).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takeuchi et al., 2019 in the previous sentence.

claim: FFI-PrPSc can promote PrPC misfolding and aggregation in vitro using PMCA and RT-QuIC assays.
source: By exploiting the recently developed Protein Misfolding Cyclic Amplification (PMCA) (Saborio et al., 2001) and Real-Time Quaking-Induced Conversion (RT-QuIC) assays (Atarashi et al., 2011), it was shown that FFI-PrPSc can promote PrPC misfolding and aggregation in vitro (Orrú et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the development of PMCA and RT-QuIC methods and their application to FFI.

claim: PMCA is able to detect traces of PrPSc present in the olfactory mucosa (OM) of a patient with FFI using the brain of bank voles (Bv109M) as a reaction substrate.
source: In this context, we have previously shown that the PMCA is able to detect traces of PrPSc present in the olfactory mucosa (OM) of a patient with FFI (at a late stage of the disease) using the brain of bank voles (Bv109M) as a reaction substrate (Redaelli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Redaelli et al., 2017).

claim: BvPrP-Tg407 mice are highly susceptible to infection by FFI-BH, FFI-BH_PMCA, and FFI-OM_PMCA.
source: Our results indicate that BvPrP-Tg407 mice are highly susceptible to infection by FFI-BH but also by the PMCA products (FFI-BH_PMCA and FFI-OM_PMCA).
evidence: This is supported by the survival data and pathological findings presented in the Results section.

claim: Animals inoculated with PMCA products developed prion isolates and neuropathological changes significantly different from those observed in mice challenged with FFI-BH.
source: Particularly, animals inoculated with PMCA products developed prion isolates and neuropathological changes significantly different from those observed in mice challenged with FFI-BH.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical and histological data presented in Figures 4, 5, 6, and 7.

claim: Through PMCA, bank vole-adapted FFI prion isolates were generated that acquired infectious properties distinct from that of the original FFI.
source: It is likely that, through PMCA, we have generated bank vole-adapted FFI prion isolates that acquired infectious properties distinct from that of the original FFI, and this resulted in the appearance of different pathological phenotypes of the disease.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, representing an inference from the data.

claim: None of the animals inoculated with AD-related samples developed prion pathology.
source: As expected, none of the animals inoculated with AD-related samples developed prion pathology.
evidence: This is supported by the absence of PrPres and pathological changes in AD-inoculated mice as shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: BvPrP-Tg407 transgenic mice express physiological levels of bank vole PrPC with methionine at codon 109 in the absence of murine PrPC.
source: These mice express physiological levels of bank vole PrPC with methionine at codon 109 in the absence of murine PrPC (Espinosa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Espinosa et al., 2016.

claim: Frozen samples of frontal cortex collected from a patient with FFID178N-129MM or a patient with AD homozygous for methionine at 129 PRNP codon were homogenized at 10% (w/v) in PBS.
source: Frozen samples of frontal cortex collected from a patient with FFID178N-129MM or a patient with AD homozygous for methionine at 129 PRNP codon were homogenized at 10% (weight/volume; w/v) in PBS.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used to prepare the inocula.

claim: Both FFI-BH and AD-BH specimens were subjected to three rounds of PMCA.
source: Both specimens were subjected to three rounds of PMCA (as described in Redaelli et al., 2017) and named FFI-BH_PMCA or AD-BH_PMCA, respectively.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: All PMCA reactions were performed using the brain of bank vole homozygous for methionine at codon 109 of the Prnp (Bv109M).
source: All PMCA reactions were performed using the brain of bank vole homozygous for methionine at codon 109 of the Prnp (Bv109M).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Prions observed in FFI-BH, FFI-BH_PMCA, and FFI-OM_PMCA showed analogous biochemical properties characterized by a predominance of the di-glycosylated PrP band and the migration of un-glycosylated one at 19 kDa.
source: Notably, the prions observed in FFI-BH, FFI-BH_PMCA, and FFI-OM_PMCA showed analogous biochemical properties that were characterized by a predominance of the di-glycosylated PrP band and the migration of un-glycosylated one at 19 kDa.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1.

claim: PrPres was not detected in FFI-OM sample before amplification.
source: As expected, we did not detect PrPres in FFI-OM sample before amplification.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 where FFI-OM shows no signal.

claim: None of the samples collected from patients with Alzheimer's disease showed a PrPres signal.
source: None of the samples collected from patients with Alzheimer's disease showed a PrPres signal.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 where all AD samples are negative.

claim: All animals inoculated with FFI-BH, FFI-BH_PMCA, and FFI-OM_PMCA succumbed to prion disease.
source: All animals inoculated with FFI-BH, FFI-BH_PMCA, and FFI-OM_PMCA (continuous lines in Figure 2) succumbed to prion disease
evidence: This is shown in the survival curve in Figure 2.

claim: Animals inoculated with AD-BH, AD-BH_PMCA, and AD-OM_PMCA did not succumb to prion disease and were sacrificed at the end of the experiment.
source: while those inoculated with AD-BH, AD-BH_PMCA, and AD-OM_PMCA did not and were sacrificed at the end of the experiment (dashed lines in Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in the survival curve in Figure 2.

claim: The clinical presentation of prion disease was similar between groups and mainly characterized by ataxia, generalized tremor, sustained hunched posture, and extensive piloerection.
source: The clinical presentation of the disease was similar between groups and mainly characterized by the presence of typical prion signs and symptoms including, ataxia, generalized tremor, sustained hunched posture, and extensive piloerection.
evidence: This describes the clinical observations made during the experiment.

claim: Animals inoculated with FFI-BH showed clinical alterations at 431 ± 58 dpi.
source: Although animals inoculated with FFI-BH showed clinical alterations earlier (431 ± 58 dpi) than those inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA (489 ± 13 dpi) and FFI-OM_PMCA (474 ± 27 dpi), the differences in the survival times did not reach a statistical significance (p=0.085, log-rank test) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Animals inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA showed clinical alterations at 489 ± 13 dpi.
source: Although animals inoculated with FFI-BH showed clinical alterations earlier (431 ± 58 dpi) than those inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA (489 ± 13 dpi) and FFI-OM_PMCA (474 ± 27 dpi), the differences in the survival times did not reach a statistical significance (p=0.085, log-rank test) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Animals inoculated with FFI-OM_PMCA showed clinical alterations at 474 ± 27 dpi.
source: Although animals inoculated with FFI-BH showed clinical alterations earlier (431 ± 58 dpi) than those inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA (489 ± 13 dpi) and FFI-OM_PMCA (474 ± 27 dpi), the differences in the survival times did not reach a statistical significance (p=0.085, log-rank test) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The differences in the survival times between FFI-BH, FFI-BH_PMCA, and FFI-OM_PMCA groups did not reach statistical significance (p=0.085).
source: Although animals inoculated with FFI-BH showed clinical alterations earlier (431 ± 58 dpi) than those inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA (489 ± 13 dpi) and FFI-OM_PMCA (474 ± 27 dpi), the differences in the survival times did not reach a statistical significance (p=0.085, log-rank test) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of survival data using log-rank test.

claim: Five out of six animals of the FFI-BH group developed a PrPres mainly characterized by a predominance of the di-glycosylated band with the un-glycosylated one migrating at 19 kDa.
source: Five out of six animals of the FFI-BH group developed a PrPres mainly characterized by a predominance of the di-glycosylated band with the un-glycosylated one migrating at 19 kDa.
evidence: This is shown in Western blot data in Figure 3a.

claim: One animal (number #5) in the FFI-BH group developed a PrPres characterized by a predominance of the mono-glycosylated band with the un-glycosylated one migrating at 19 kDa.
source: Unexpectedly, in one of these animals (the number #5), we have detected a PrPres characterized by a predominance of the mono-glycosylated band with the un-glycosylated one migrating at 19 kDa.
evidence: This is shown in Western blot data in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: All the animals inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA showed a PrPres signal characterized by a predominance of the di-glycosylated band with the un-glycosylated one migrating at 19 kDa.
source: All the animals inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA showed a PrPres signal characterized by a predominance of the di-glycosylated band with the un-glycosylated one migrating at 19 kDa (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is shown in Western blot data in Figure 3b.

claim: Animals inoculated with FFI-OM_PMCA showed PrPres characterized by a predominance of the di-glycosylated band with the un-glycosylated one migrating at 19 kDa.
source: Similar findings were observed in the brains of animals inoculated with FFI-OM_PMCA (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is shown in Western blot data in Figure 3c.

claim: Animal number #1 of the FFI-OM_PMCA group was characterized by the presence of two faint un-glycosylated PrPres fragments detectable only with the N-terminal 6D11 antibody.
source: However, animal number #1 of the FFI-OM_PMCA group was characterized by the presence of two faint un-glycosylated PrPres fragments detectable only with the use of the N-terminal 6D11 antibody. This difference could not be appreciated with the use of the C-terminal Sha31 antibody where a single un-glycosylated band migrating at 19 kDa was detected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Western blot data in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: All prions generated in the brain of BvPrP-Tg407 mice migrated at 19 kDa after PNGase F treatment, regardless of the inoculum.
source: To better analyze the migration profile of the un-glycosylated PrP bands, we have performed PNGase F experiments and observed that all prions generated in the brain of BvPrP-Tg407 mice migrated at 19 kDa, regardless of the inoculum (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is shown in Western blot data in Figure 3d.

claim: No PrPres was found in the brain of BvPrP-Tg407 mice inoculated with AD-BH, AD-BH_PMCA, and AD-OM_PMCA.
source: No PrPres was found in the brain of BvPrP-Tg407 mice inoculated with AD-BH, AD-BH_PMCA, and AD-OM_PMCA.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data in Figure 3.

claim: Prions found in the brains of animals inoculated with FFI-BH were significantly more resistant to proteolytic digestion than those found in the brains of animals inoculated with either FFI-BH_PMCA or FFI-OM_PMCA.
source: As shown in Figure 4, prions found in the brains of animals inoculated with FFI-BH were significantly more resistant to proteolytic digestion than those found in the brains of animals inoculated with either FFI-BH_PMCA or FFI-OM_PMCA (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is shown in PK resistance assay data in Figure 4a.

claim: The PK-resistance profile of the PrPres found in animals inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA and FFI-OM_PMCA was comparable.
source: Conversely, the PK-resistance profile of the PrPres found in animals inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA and FFI-OM_PMCA was comparable.
evidence: This is shown in PK resistance assay data in Figure 4a.

claim: PMCA might have favored the in vitro amplification/selection of a similar prion isolate from brain and OM of FFI patients.
source: This suggests that the PMCA might have favored the in vitro amplification/selection of a similar prion isolate from brain and OM of FFI patients, which then resulted in a homogeneous pathological picture of the disease in both animals' groups (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is an interpretation/inference from the PK resistance data.

claim: Prions found in the brains of FFI-BH_PMCA and FFI-OM_PMCA-inoculated animals were more stable than those found in the brain of FFI-BH-challenged mice.
source: Results of this analysis are shown in Figure 4 and confirmed that prions found in the brains of FFI-BH_PMCA and FFI-OM_PMCA-inoculated animals were more stable than those found in the brain of FFI-BH-challenged mice.
evidence: This is shown in conformational stability assay data in Figure 4b.

claim: The difference in conformational stability between prions from FFI-BH_PMCA/FFI-OM_PMCA-inoculated animals and FFI-BH-challenged mice was statistically significant.
source: Notably, this difference was statistically significant, thus supporting the hypothesis that PMCA could have amplified a PrPSc with distinctive biochemical and pathological features than that typically present in the FFI brain homogenate, finally leading to the development of different pathological changes in FFI-BH_PMCA and FFI-OM_PMCA groups of mice (also in this case, animal number #5 was excluded from the analysis) (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is shown in conformational stability assay data in Figure 4b with statistical analysis.

claim: After amplification, the PrPSc did not change the PK-resistant properties compared to FFI-BH.
source: We have found that, after amplification, the PrPSc did not change the PK-resistant properties (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a) but became significantly more stable towards Gdn-HCl treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: After amplification, the PrPSc became significantly more stable towards Gdn-HCl treatment compared to FFI-BH.
source: We have found that, after amplification, the PrPSc did not change the PK-resistant properties (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a) but became significantly more stable towards Gdn-HCl treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b.

claim: PMCA has slightly altered the biochemical properties of the original FFI-PrPSc, especially in terms of conformational stability.
source: Thus, we have observed that the PMCA has indeed slightly altered the biochemical properties of the original FFI-PrPSc, especially in terms of conformational stability.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: All groups of prion-inoculated animals showed mild spongiform changes mainly affecting the thalamus, the striatum, and to a lesser extent the frontal cortex.
source: All groups of prion-inoculated animals showed mild spongiform changes mainly affecting the thalamus, the striatum, and to a lesser extent the frontal cortex.
evidence: This is shown in histological data in Figure 5a.

claim: Spongiform changes were slightly more pronounced in the brain of mice challenged with FFI-BH compared to that of the other groups.
source: In particular, these alterations were slightly more pronounced in the brain of mice challenged with FFI-BH compared to that of the other groups.
evidence: This is shown in histological data in Figure 5a.

claim: No vacuolation was observed in animals inoculated with AD-related samples.
source: No vacuolation was observed in animals inoculated with AD-related samples (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is shown in histological data in Figure 5a.

claim: The ventricles of most of the animals inoculated with FFI-BH were significantly enlarged.
source: Notably, the ventricles of most of the animals inoculated with FFI-BH were significantly enlarged (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is shown in macroscopic findings in Figure 5b.

claim: Severe glial activation was observed in all groups of mice inoculated with FFI-related materials and mostly affected the thalamus.
source: Severe glial activation was observed in all groups of mice inoculated with FFI-related materials and mostly affected the thalamus.
evidence: This is shown in immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5b and Figure 7.

claim: Animals inoculated with FFI-BH showed a synaptic and diffuse pattern of PrPres deposition that mainly affected the thalamus, the striatum, and the deep layers of the frontal cortex.
source: Animals inoculated with FFI-BH showed a synaptic and diffuse pattern of PrPres deposition that mainly affected the thalamus, the striatum, and the deep layers of the frontal cortex.
evidence: This is shown in immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6.

claim: Plaque-like deposits (negative at ThS staining) were found in the striatum and sometimes in the frontal cortex of animals inoculated with FFI-BH.
source: Plaque-like deposits (negative at ThS staining) were also found in the striatum and sometimes in the frontal cortex (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in immunohistochemistry and ThS staining data in Figure 6 and supplements.

claim: Animals #5 and #6 of the FFI-BH group did not show any PrPres detectable by immunohistochemistry even in the thalamus and striatum.
source: Notably, animals #5 and #6 of this group did not show any PrPres detectable by means of immunohistochemistry (although we could see a PrPres signal by Wb) even in the thalamus and striatum where we observed a mild vacuolation and significant astroglial activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mice inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA or FFI-OM_PMCA did not show any synaptic PrPres deposition but only focal and plaque-like aggregates, negative at ThS staining.
source: Mice inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA or FFI-OM_PMCA did not show any synaptic PrPres deposition but only focal and plaque-like aggregates, negative at ThS staining (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 3) prevalently affecting thalamus, striatum, and cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is shown in immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: PrPres deposits were more abundant in animals inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA compared to those inoculated with FFI-OM_PMCA.
source: These deposits were more abundant in animals inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA compared to those inoculated with FFI-OM_PMCA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: No PrPres immunoreactivity was found in the brain of mice inoculated with AD-BH, AD-BH_PMCA, or AD-OM_PMCA.
source: As expected, no PrPres immunoreactivity was found in the brain of mice inoculated with AD-BH, AD-BH_PMCA, or AD-OM_PMCA (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: RT-QuIC analysis confirmed that the brains of animals inoculated with FFI-BH, FFI-BH_PMCA, and FFI-OM_PMCA were able to promote the aggregation of recBvPrP90-231 with high efficiency.
source: RT-QuIC analysis of BvPrP-Tg407 mice confirmed that the brains of animals inoculated with FFI-BH, FFI-BH_PMCA, and FFI-OM_PMCA were able to promote the aggregation of recBvPrP90-231 with high efficiency.
evidence: This is shown in RT-QuIC data in Figure 8.

claim: The aggregation kinetics in RT-QuIC were very rapid and the threshold of fluorescence was crossed by all FFI samples before 10 hr, regardless of the inocula.
source: The aggregation kinetics were in general very rapid and the threshold of fluorescence was crossed by all samples before 10 hr, regardless of the inocula (Figure 8).
evidence: This is shown in RT-QuIC data in Figure 8.

claim: Animals inoculated with AD-BH, AD-BH_PMCA, and AD-OM_PMCA induced recBvPrP90-231 aggregation after 18 hr and were considered negative.
source: Animals inoculated with AD-BH, AD-BH_PMCA, and AD-OM_PMCA induced recBvPrP90-231 aggregation after 18 hr and were considered negative.
evidence: This is shown in RT-QuIC data in Figure 8.

claim: This is the second study showing that PrPSc amplified by PMCA from peripheral tissues of patients with prion diseases is infectious when challenged in susceptible mice.
source: This is the second study showing that PrPSc amplified by PMCA from peripheral tissues of patients with prion diseases is infectious when challenged in susceptible mice.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the work in the context of existing literature.

claim: BvPrP-Tg407 mice do not develop spontaneous pathology.
source: Remarkably, BvPrP-Tg407 mice do not develop spontaneous pathology (Espinosa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Espinosa et al., 2016.

claim: A very recent study showed that OM of patients with sporadic CJD are able to induce prion disease when challenged in transgenic mice overexpressing the human PrP with methionine at codon 129 (Tg66).
source: However, a very recent study (Raymond et al., 2020) showed that OM of patients with sporadic CJD are able to induce prion disease when challenged in transgenic mice overexpressing the human PrP with methionine at codon 129 (Tg66).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Raymond et al., 2020.

claim: In the Raymond et al. study, only a small percentage of animals developed the disease, suggesting that the infectivity in OM is very low.
source: In this study, only a small percentage of animals developed the disease, thus suggesting that the infectivity in OM is very low.
evidence: This is an interpretation of results from Raymond et al., 2020.

claim: The BvPrP can be converted into PrPSc by a number of human and animal prion strains with high efficiency.
source: It is known that the BvPrP can be converted into PrPSc by a number of human and animal prion strains with high efficiency (Watts et al., 2014; Nonno et al., 2006; Agrimi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Transgenic mice expressing BvPrP with methionine or isoleucine at codon 109 developed prion pathology with PrPres characterized by a predominance of the di-glycosylated band, even when challenged with prion strains with the mono-glycosylated predominant PrP band.
source: For instance, upon inoculation with different human and animal prion strains, transgenic mice expressing the BvPrP with methionine or isoleucine at codon 109 (TgM109 or TgI109, respectively) developed prion pathology and all generated PrPres were characterized by a predominance of the di-glycosylated band, even in those challenged with human or animal prion strains with the mono-glycosylated predominant PrP band (e.g., sporadic CJD or Rocky Mountain Laboratory prion strain (RML)) (Watts et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Watts et al., 2014.

claim: Transgenic mice expressing BvPrP with isoleucine at codon 109 and the D178 mutation spontaneously developed prion diseases with the presence of a PrPres with a predominant di-glycosylated band.
source: This has been observed also in transgenic mice expressing BvPrP with isoleucine at codon 109 and the D178 mutation that spontaneously developed prion diseases with the presence of a PrPres with a predominant di-glycosylated band (Watts et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Watts et al., 2016.

claim: A significant enlargement of the ventricular spaces was observed in the brain of many FFI-BH-inoculated mice.
source: Another alteration that we have noticed in the brain of many FFI-BH-inoculated mice, as previously published (Jackson et al., 2009), was a significant enlargement of the ventricular spaces.
evidence: This is supported by histological observations and citation to Jackson et al., 2009.

claim: Ventricular enlargement was not found in the brain of mice inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA and FFI-OM_PMCA.
source: This change was not found in the brain of mice inoculated with FFI-BH_PMCA and FFI-OM_PMCA.
evidence: This is based on histological observations.

claim: There is compelling evidence that some human prion strains originally believed to be 'pure' are instead composed by a mixture of PrPSc variants.
source: There is a compelling evidence that some human prion strains originally believed to be 'pure' are instead composed by a mixture of PrPSc variants (Cassard et al., 2020; Kobayashi et al., 2011; Bishop et al., 2010; Morales et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: At least two distinct prion strains can be responsible for FFID178N-129MM, one associated with the typical clinical presentation and the other associated with an atypical phenotype.
source: Interestingly, a very recent publication of the group of Kitamoto Tetsuyuki showed that even the FFID178N-129MM strain might not be pure and that at least two distinct prion strains can be responsible for the disease, one associated with the typical clinical presentation of the disease and the other associated with an atypical phenotype (Takeuchi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takeuchi et al., 2019.

claim: The fact that PMCA products are as infectious as the FFI brain homogenate raises major biosafety concerns that require the adoption of specific precautions when manipulating amplified material.
source: The fact that the PMCA products are as infectious as the FFI brain homogenate raises major biosafety concerns that require the adoption of specific precautions when manipulating amplified material (Bistaffa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results with citation to biosafety considerations.

claim: RT-QuIC assay was found not to replicate biohazardous prions in vitro.
source: For diagnostic purpose, a safer alternative is represented by the RT-QuIC assay that, according to the latest evidence, was found not to replicate biohazardous prions in vitro (Raymond et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Raymond et al., 2020.

claim: The OM of FFI patients contains potentially infectious prions.
source: Although with some experimental constraints, we showed that the OM of FFI patients contains potentially infectious prions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the transmission data.

claim: All inoculated animals developed pathology in the thalamus, which is also the area typically affected in the brain of patients with FFI.
source: All inoculated animals developed pathology in the thalamus, which is also the area typically affected in the brain of patients with FFI.
evidence: This is based on histological observations and comparison with human FFI pathology.

claim: The glycoform ratio of the PrPres in inoculated mice was similar to that found in the brain of diseased FFI patients.
source: Moreover, the glycoform ratio of the PrPres was similar to that found in the brain of diseased patients.
evidence: This is based on Western blot analysis comparing mouse and human samples.

claim: Some important FFI-PrPSc features might have been lost due to the passage of the species barrier.
source: Hence, some important FFI-PrPSc features might have been lost due to the passage of the species barrier, as already shown by several experimental transmission studies described in the literature (Bartz et al., 2000; Peretz et al., 2002; Bruce et al., 1994).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to studies on species barrier effects.
